evidence.source: 漢字構形資料庫（中央研究院）
evidence.field: 字形演變 / 字形說明
evidence.text: The entry displays 手 under bronze inscriptions, Chu manuscripts, and Small Seal script, with a bronze inscription indexed as 集成09728. Its account interprets the graph as a human hand, with the upper branches representing five fingers and the lower part the arm. The displayed sequence does not include an oracle-bone form.
evidence.title: 漢字「手」：字形演變

evidence.source: 徐富昌, National Taiwan University e-book chapter
evidence.text: The chapter states that this graph-form 手 is absent from oracle-bone inscriptions, distinguishes oracle-bone graphs 𠂇 and 𠂆, and describes bronze 手 forms as showing the fingers, palm, and arm from the front. This qualifies broader claims that 手 itself is securely attested on oracle bones; the excerpt supplies no specific date for the cited bronzes.
evidence.title: 徐富昌 chapter (PDF)

evidence.source: 書法圖集, citing bronze inscription catalogues and transmitted dictionaries
evidence.text: The page lists 手 examples from Western Zhou middle-period bronzes (including 逆鐘, 集成63, and 曶壺蓋, 集成9728), a Western Zhou late-period vessel, Warring States Chu and Qin materials, Qin manuscripts, and Western Han and Eastern Han clerical forms. It quotes Shuowen: “手，拳也。象形。凡手之屬皆从手。𠂿，古文手。” The page records the received graph forms, but does not document semantic contexts for the bronze occurrences.
evidence.title: 手 字形演变

evidence.source: 漢典, Shuowen entry and commentary
evidence.field: 說文解字; 說文解字注
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen definition is 拳也 (“fist”), classifies 手 as pictographic, and says graphs in the 手 category derive from it. Duan Yucai explains this as hand when extended and fist when curled, treating the terms as mutually explanatory. This is an early lexicographic analysis, not independent proof of the graph's original spoken-word history.
evidence.title: 手 shǒu - 汉典

evidence.text: The entry cites 易·說卦 (“艮為手”) and 詩·邶風·北風 (“攜手同行”) for the hand sense, and 詩·邶風·擊鼓 (“執子之手”) for hand in a phrase. These are transmitted textual citations, not independently dated excavated attestations; this page does not establish the date of the wording or a chronological path from the bodily noun to later senses.
evidence.title: 手 shǒu - 汉典

evidence.text: The dictionary separately records extensions such as “person skilled at a task” (with a citation to 宋書), handwriting (漢書), and 手 as a verb “hold” (公羊傳). These illustrate attested later uses; the page does not demonstrate when or through what intermediate steps each extension arose. Shuowen's gloss 拳 should therefore not be treated as a chronology of senses.
evidence.title: 手 shǒu - 汉典

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction, public table version 1.1
evidence.text: The authors identify their table as Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstructions and distinguish its OC reconstruction column from its Middle Chinese transcription column; the latter is a notation for information in Middle Chinese sources, not itself an Old Chinese reconstruction. The local specified Baxter–Sagart row for 手 reads py shǒu, MC syuwX, OC *n̥uʔ, gloss hand. The local row agrees with the published system's notation as used here; no second character is proposed as a sound component for 手.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1

evidence.source: 金真姬, 常用漢字二百字探源
evidence.field: 手字形探源; 字義探源
evidence.text: The study states that 手 is not seen in oracle-bone inscriptions and that 金文編 records eleven forms. It describes the bronze graph as a hand, with finger branches above and an arm below; it identifies the basic meaning as human hand and treats Shuowen’s 拳 (“fist”) as an extended sense. The page’s form table includes 昌壺 under Western Zhou and later Zhou and manuscript forms.
evidence.title: 常用漢字二百字探源

evidence.text: The page catalogs 手 forms from Western Zhou middle-period bronzes including 逆鐘 (集成63), 無㠱簋, and 曶壺蓋 (集成9728), then Western Zhou late-period bronzes, Warring States Chu and Qin forms, Qin slips, Han slips, and later clerical forms. These labels date the cited artifact traditions, but the page does not give semantic contexts for the cited bronze occurrences.

search_audit.outcome: Searched and opened a scholarly paleographic study, a character-specific form chart, exact Commons descriptions for seal, bronze and great-seal candidates, the Sinica and NTU records, and the official Unihan endpoint. gaps: The earliest securely identified 手 graph in sources inspected here is in Western Zhou middle-period bronze materials; no earliest individual inscription date or semantic context for those graph occurrences was verified.

The record presents a disagreement in coverage: one chart catalogs bronze and later forms without an oracle-bone section, while the NTU discussion explicitly says 手 is absent in oracle bones and distinguishes 𠂇/𠂆. No directly inspectable oracle-bone corpus entry was found to adjudicate beyond that.

The Sinica chart's displayed account calls the top branches five fingers and the lower part an arm; an NTU paleographic discussion instead describes fingers, palm, and arm as a front view. Exact graphic anatomy is an interpretation, not separately verified by visual inspection of a primary inscription here.

No inspected source established the spoken-word history of 手, the proposed relationship to PST wing/hand vocabulary, the Burmese comparison, or Schuessler's derivation from 收; these are outside the demonstrated graphic analysis.

The cited classical and dictionary examples provide sense evidence but not a secure dated sequence of semantic extensions. Distinguish quoted classical loci from independently dated manuscripts or inscriptions.

No sound component exists in the dossier's pictographic analysis; consequently no component pronunciation comparison or phonetic-role claim is warranted.

The inspected paleographic study reports no oracle-bone 手 graph and identifies bronze forms, including a Western Zhou form, but no directly dated earliest inscription with its semantic context was verified.

Graphic anatomy is an interpretation: the source describes five finger branches and an arm; an alternative cited dossier account mentions fingers, palm and arm. No photographed inscription was visually examined in this research stage.

The cited bronze examples establish forms and approximate artifact-period labels, not independently dated semantic uses. The early hand sense is supported by later lexicography and the study’s analysis, not by a located excavated text context.

Classical examples and later extensions in the dossier remain transmitted dictionary citations; this search did not independently establish dates or a chronological semantic pathway for skilled person, handwriting, or ‘hold’. Shuowen’s gloss 拳 is not a chronology.
